topic.title: Right-angled triangles (Pythagoras' theorem)
topic.blurb: Using Pythagoras' theorem to find sides and test right angles.

methods.description: Find the marked or stated right angle, then name the side opposite it by its side label, endpoint letters or real-world part. Orientation and context do not change this identification method.

When a triangle is explicitly known to be right-angled and side lengths are given, the longest side is the hypotenuse, including when the angle is not marked. Do not apply this rule to a triangle of unknown type or calculate using Pythagoras.

sourceReview.observation: Read complete actual teaching58–105 and Key Ideas. It defines the hypotenuse as the longest side opposite the right angle and asks for the90-degree/square/longest/opposite ideas. Actually inspected images4–11:4has marked conventional triangle withh;5/6/7each contain three differently oriented triangles and right-angle squares;8is a rectangle split diagonally;11shows a triangle on extended vertical/horizontal lines. Images9/10are unmarked and do not establish that their triangles are right-angled; no hypotenuse is inferred merely from their appearance. The Markdown repeats composite images across multiple named cells, so no unverified teaching part-to-panel correspondence is claimed. Only identifiable source panels are adapted. Identification and known-right-triangle longest-side recognition govern; no Pythagoras calculation or advanced side terminology is taught.

This adapts identifiable teaching rotations/short square markers and numerical-free source side labelling, rather than claiming a separate method for every orientation. Kept generic theory illustrations separate. The first theory hypotenuse word was floating inside the triangle; now it labels the actualhside. Used the source’s two shorter sides wording instead of legs throughout theory/distractor explanations. Corrected unshown vertexA references and inaccurate down/left orientation descriptions without changing side labels or answers.
